title: Pulled Pork Tacos
subtitle: Smoky slow-cooked pork shoulder in warm corn tortillas
excerpt: Pork shoulder cooked low and slow with smoked paprika, chilli, and brown sugar until it pulls apart in strands, then loaded into corn tortillas with pickled red onion and slaw. Serves a crowd with minimal work.
sourceNotes: Pulled pork tacos: a Tex-Mex and American barbecue fusion dish that became popular across the US from the 1990s. Slow-cooked pulled pork is rooted in American Southern barbecue traditions (particularly Carolinian and Texan); the taco format is borrowed from Tex-Mex cooking. Drawn from standard American home-cooking and barbecue sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Pulled pork freezes well for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat in a covered pan with a splash of stock or water.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch; the pork reheats well and works in sandwiches, rice bowls, and loaded fries.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pork can be cooked and pulled a day ahead. Reheat covered with a splash of the cooking juices.

content.text: Pulled pork tacos are corn tortillas loaded with smoky slow-braised pork that has been shredded into long, tender strands, then topped with pickled red onion and a sharp slaw. Pork shoulder needs 4 hours at a low heat to become properly tender; once it does, it pulls apart with almost no effort. The payoff for the wait is a large batch that keeps and reheats well.
A casserole dish with a tight lid keeps the pork moist over the long braise. The quick-pickled red onion is ready in 20 minutes and cuts through the richness of the meat.
Heat the oven to 150°C. Mix the smoked paprika, chilli powder, cumin, dark brown sugar, garlic powder, and 1 tsp salt. Rub the mixture all over the pork shoulder.
Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a casserole dish over high heat. Sear the pork for 3-4 minutes on each side until deep brown. Remove from the heat.

Pour {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock and {{cider-vinegar}} of cider vinegar around the pork (not over the top; keep the crust dry). Cover tightly and cook in the oven at 150°C for 3.5-4 hours. The pork should pull apart easily with two forks when ready.
Rest the pork in the dish for 15 minutes before pulling. Remove any large pieces of fat and shred the meat into long strands with two forks. Mix the strands through the cooking juices.
Make the pickled onion and slaw
While the pork rests, toss the sliced red onion with the lime juice and a pinch of salt. Leave for at least 20 minutes; the onion will turn pink and mellow in flavour.
Toss the shredded cabbage with the coriander and a squeeze of lime. Season with salt.
Warm the corn tortillas in a dry pan. Fill each with pulled pork, slaw, pickled onion, and a spoonful of soured cream. Add jalapeño if using.

items.symptom: Pork won't pull apart after 4 hours
items.cause: The oven ran too cool, or the lid didn't seal tightly
items.fix: Return to the oven for another 30-45 minutes. Pork shoulder varies; a 1.5 kg piece may need up to 4.5 hours. The meat should yield with almost no resistance when it's ready.

items.cause: Not enough liquid in the pot, or pork pulled from the dish without mixing back through the juices
items.fix: Add a splash of stock if the pot looks dry at the 2-hour check. Always mix the pulled meat through the braising juices before serving.

items.cause: Too much liquid added, or the pork sat in liquid rather than above it
items.fix: The liquid level should come only a third of the way up the pork; it's a braise, not a boil. The crust on the submerged sides will soften, but the top stays intact.

items.symptom: Pickled onion still tastes raw and harsh
items.cause: Not enough lime juice, or not left long enough
items.fix: The onion needs at least 20 minutes in the lime juice to mellow. Use enough juice to cover the slices; a little extra won't hurt.

content.text: Pulled pork tacos are the crossing point of two American traditions: Southern barbecue slow-cooked pork and the Tex-Mex taco. The combination became popular in US casual dining from the 1990s. British home cooks have taken it up too, since pork shoulder is cheap and suits a weekend braise. The taco is a practical wrapper for something that would otherwise need sides and cutlery.
